title: Proving HLA Linkage: Type 1 Diabetes, Narcolepsy and the LOD Score
summary: Use expected sibling haplotype sharing and the LOD score to judge linkage, then see how HLA class II haplotypes shape type 1 diabetes risk and why DQB1*06:02 protects against diabetes yet is nearly universal in narcolepsy with cataplexy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 51 Hits 5 and 8 and Traps 5 and 6. Sib-pair expectations and LOD definitions from Ott 2015 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Gorman 2012; T1D linkage from Concannon 2009; T1D haplotypes and twin data from Noble 2011 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Pociot 2010; narcolepsy from Tafti 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Miyagawa 2019. Discrepancies: the reviewer’s “twin concordance ≤50%” omits that concordance rises with follow-up (65% by age 60, Noble 2011; register flag rv-t1d-twin-concordance); the narcolepsy NPV >99% applies to narcolepsy with cataplexy (type 1) and was calculated from a case-control sample, while only 30–50% of type 2 patients carry DQB1*06:02 (Miyagawa 2019; register flag rv-narcolepsy-dqb1-type). Not taught as fact: the specific 60/35/5 sharing figures in diabetic sib pairs (only qualitative excess sharing and the LOD of 213 are taught), and the reviewer’s 15–25% carrier figure (the lesson uses about 20% for Europe, Tafti 2014; Miyagawa 2019 gives 12–25% for the DRB1*15:01-DQB1*06:02 haplotype).

objectives: State the expected 25/50/25 haplotype sharing between siblings and explain why excess sharing in affected sib pairs is evidence of linkage.
Interpret LOD scores: LOD ≥3 (1000:1 odds) for linkage, ≤−2 for exclusion, about 3.3 for genome-wide multipoint scans.
Name the main HLA risk and protective haplotypes in type 1 diabetes, and explain why DQB1*06:02 typing rules out, but does not diagnose, narcolepsy with cataplexy.

scenes.title: Two puzzling reports
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Report 1: a small family study of type 1 diabetes finds that affected sibling pairs share both HLA haplotypes more often than expected, and a marker gives a LOD score of 1.2; a student writes “linkage proven”. Report 2: a sleepy teenager without cataplexy is HLA-DQB1*06:02 positive; a note reads “narcolepsy confirmed”. Question token: “Proof, or not yet?”

cues.text: Two reports land on your bench. A family study of type 1 diabetes finds a marker with a LOD score of 1.2, and a student writes: linkage proven.
A sleepy teenager tests positive for HLA-DQB1 star 06:02, and a note says: narcolepsy confirmed.
Is either report proof, or not yet?

scenes.title: Sharing by descent and the LOD score
scenes.altText: Schematic sibship diagram. Two full siblings are expected to share 2, 1 or 0 parental haplotypes identical by descent in proportions 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25 (Ott 2015). Affected sib-pair analysis is an allele-sharing method: if a region is linked to the disease, affected siblings share it more often than these proportions. LOD card: the LOD score is the base-10 logarithm of the odds (likelihood ratio) for linkage versus no linkage; single-point LOD ≥3 for autosomes = 1000:1 odds, the accepted threshold; LOD ≤ −2 excludes linkage; for multipoint genome-wide scans 3.3 corresponds to genome-wide significance (Gorman 2012; Ott 2015).

cues.text: Two brothers or sisters are expected to share two, one or zero parental haplotypes by descent in a ratio of one quarter, one half and one quarter.
Affected sib-pair analysis asks whether siblings who both have the disease share a region more often than that. Excess sharing points to a linked gene.
The strength of linkage is expressed as a LOD score: the base ten logarithm of the odds for linkage versus no linkage. A LOD of three means odds of one thousand to one, the accepted threshold.
A LOD of minus two or lower excludes linkage, and genome-wide multipoint scans usually ask for about 3.3.

scenes.title: HLA and type 1 diabetes
scenes.altText: Linkage card: in 2,496 multiplex families (Type 1 Diabetes Genetics Consortium), the HLA region on 6p21.3 gave LOD = 213.2, the only region reaching significant linkage (Concannon 2009). Risk card (Noble 2011): DR3 (DRB1*03:01-DQA1*05:01-DQB1*02:01) and DR4 haplotypes carrying DQB1*03:02 (DQ8), with DRB1*04:05, 04:01 and 04:02 among predisposing DR4 alleles; DR3/DR4 heterozygotes carry the highest risk (OR about 16.6). Protection card: DRB1*15:01-DQA1*01:02-DQB1*06:02 (DR2) gives almost complete, dominant protection (OR 0.03). Twins card: monozygotic concordance about 50% vs about 8% for dizygotic twins (Pociot 2010), rising to 65% by age 60 in long follow-up (Noble 2011); the HLA region explains roughly 40–50% of familial clustering.

cues.text: In type 1 diabetes the HLA region is linked beyond any doubt. In almost 2,500 families with affected siblings, it gave a LOD score of 213, the only region to reach significant linkage.
The main risk haplotypes are DR3, carrying DQB1 star 02:01, and DR4 haplotypes carrying DQB1 star 03:02, also called DQ8. A DR3 plus DR4 heterozygote has the highest risk.
The DR15 haplotype, DRB1 star 15:01 with DQB1 star 06:02, protects almost completely, and the protection is dominant.

Yet identical twins are concordant only about half the time, rising to about two thirds with follow-up to age sixty. HLA explains roughly half the family clustering; other genes and the environment matter.

scenes.title: The same allele in narcolepsy
scenes.altText: Narcolepsy cards. Tafti 2014 (European cohort, narcolepsy with cataplexy; 1,218 patients and 3,541 country-matched controls): more than 98% of patients carry DQB1*06:02 versus about 20% of the general European population; from that case-control sample the authors calculate a negative predictive value of 99.32% and a positive predictive value of 65.68%; homozygosity doubled the risk; DQB1*06:03 (OR 0.17) and DQB1*05:01 (OR 0.56) were protective. Miyagawa 2019: almost all type 1 narcolepsy (with cataplexy, low orexin) patients carry DQB1*06:02, but only 30–50% of type 2 (without cataplexy) patients; the allele is not sufficient; DRB1*15:01 and DQB1*06:02 are in almost complete linkage disequilibrium in European and East Asian populations, so within those populations the primary allele cannot be separated, although the concordance of DQB1*06:02 across different DRB1 haplotypes points to DQB1 rather than DRB1. Contrast token: the same haplotype protects against T1D and predisposes to narcolepsy. Hook answer card.

cues.text: Now the same allele in a different disease. In a European study of narcolepsy with cataplexy, more than ninety-eight percent of patients carried DQB1 star 06:02, against about twenty percent of the general population.

So a negative result makes this form of narcolepsy very unlikely: the authors calculated a negative predictive value above ninety-nine percent from that case-control sample. Two copies doubled the risk, and DQB1 star 06:03 was protective.
But narcolepsy without cataplexy carries the allele in only thirty to fifty percent of patients, and a positive result alone never makes the diagnosis.
Back to the hook: a LOD of 1.2 is far below three, so linkage is not proven; and DQB1 star 06:02 is common in healthy people, so narcolepsy is not confirmed.

props.title: Hook answer: not yet
lines: Same haplotype: T1D shield, narcolepsy risk

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A significant LOD score is anything above 1” (✓ LOD ≥3 = 1000:1 odds; LOD 1 is only 10:1); “Excess HLA sharing in affected sib pairs means nothing” (✓ sharing above the expected 25/50/25 is the evidence for linkage, and HLA gave LOD 213 in T1D families); “DQB1*06:02 positive = narcolepsy” (✓ about 20% of healthy Europeans carry it; a negative result rules out narcolepsy with cataplexy).

cues.text: Trap one: any LOD above one is significant. No: a LOD of three, odds of one thousand to one, is needed. One means only ten to one.
Trap two: extra HLA sharing between affected siblings means nothing. No: sharing above the expected one quarter, one half, one quarter is the evidence for linkage.
Trap three: DQB1 star 06:02 means narcolepsy. No: about one in five healthy Europeans carry it. It rules out; it does not rule in.

props.title: ✗ “DQB1*06:02 = narcolepsy.”
lines: ✓ ≈ 20% of healthy Europeans carry it; rule-out test

scenes.title: One is noise, three is news
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “ONE is noise, THREE is news: a LOD of 3 means a thousand to one. And 06:02 is a double agent: it SHIELDS the pancreas from type 1 diabetes but OPENS the door to narcolepsy.” Tokens: LOD 3 = 1000:1 · siblings 25/50/25 · 06:02 double agent. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: one is noise, three is news; a LOD of three means a thousand to one. And DQB1 star 06:02 is a double agent: it shields the pancreas from type 1 diabetes but opens the door to narcolepsy.
Where it breaks: genome-wide scans may need about 3.3; the X chromosome uses a lower single-point threshold; and the double agent is a haplotype effect, not a guarantee of either outcome.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Siblings share 25/50/25 · affected-pair excess = linkage · LOD ≥3 (1000:1) · HLA LOD 213 in T1D”, “DR3/DR4 risk · DRB1*15:01-DQB1*06:02 protects in T1D · DQB1*06:02 in >98% of narcolepsy with cataplexy, ≈20% of healthy people”.

cues.text: Excess HLA sharing between affected siblings and a LOD score of at least three establish linkage, and the DQB1 star 06:02 haplotype that almost completely protects against type 1 diabetes is carried by nearly all patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy, so a negative test rules that form out but a positive test proves nothing.

props.label: 06:02: protects in T1D · > 98% in narcolepsy with cataplexy

explanation.what: Plain language: brothers and sisters inherit one of two chromosome 6 copies from each parent, so by chance they match on both copies a quarter of the time. If siblings who both have a disease match far more often, a gene in that region probably matters. A LOD score measures how strong that evidence is. In type 1 diabetes some HLA types raise risk and one protects strongly; the same protective type is almost always present in narcolepsy with cataplexy. Scientific terms: identity by descent (IBD), affected sib-pair analysis, LOD score, linkage, HLA haplotype, DR3, DR4-DQ8, DRB1*15:01-DQB1*06:02, monozygotic concordance, narcolepsy type 1 and type 2, negative predictive value.
explanation.why: Unlinked regions are shared by siblings in Mendelian proportions; a disease gene drags its region into excess sharing among affected relatives. Because linkage is tested at many positions, the bar is high: odds of 1000:1. HLA class II molecules shape which peptides T cells see, which is one reason particular haplotypes raise or lower autoimmune risk; incomplete twin concordance shows HLA is necessary context, not destiny.
explanation.measure: Sib sharing 2/1/0 haplotypes: 0.25/0.5/0.25. LOD = log10 of the likelihood ratio, linkage vs no linkage; ≥3 (autosomal single-point) = 1000:1; ≤−2 excludes; multipoint genome-wide ≈3.3. T1D: HLA LOD 213.2 in 2,496 families; DR3/DR4 OR ≈16.6; DR15-DQ6 OR 0.03; MZ concordance ≈50% (DZ ≈8%), 65% by age 60. Narcolepsy with cataplexy: DQB1*06:02 >98% vs ≈20% of the general European population; NPV 99.32% and PPV 65.68% calculated from that case-control sample; homozygosity doubles risk; DQB1*06:03 OR 0.17.
explanation.differs: Expected vs excess sharing; LOD 1 (10:1) vs 3 (1000:1); risk (DR3, DR4-DQ8) vs protective (DR15-DQ6) haplotypes in T1D; narcolepsy type 1 (nearly all DQB1*06:02) vs type 2 (30–50%).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify the LOD threshold, interpret affected sib-pair sharing, name the protective T1D haplotype, and state that DQB1*06:02 negativity argues against narcolepsy with cataplexy while positivity proves nothing.

questions.stem: A two-point linkage analysis between a marker and a disease gives a maximum LOD score of 1.2. How should it be interpreted?

options.text: Not significant; a LOD of 3 (1000:1 odds) is the accepted threshold for linkage
options.rationale: Correct. A LOD of 1.2 is odds of only about 16:1; linkage needs a LOD of at least 3.

options.text: Significant linkage, because any LOD above 1 is significant
options.rationale: Incorrect. A LOD of 1 corresponds to only 10:1 odds.
Incorrect. Exclusion requires a LOD of −2 or lower.

options.text: The marker is the disease gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. Even significant linkage shows only that a disease gene lies nearby.

questions.stem: In families with type 1 diabetes, affected sibling pairs share both HLA haplotypes far more often than 25%. What does this indicate?

options.text: Evidence for linkage of type 1 diabetes to the HLA region
options.rationale: Correct. Siblings are expected to share 2/1/0 haplotypes 25/50/25%; excess sharing in affected pairs signals linkage, and HLA gave a LOD of 213 in a large family study.

options.text: Nothing, because siblings always share HLA haplotypes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only 25% of sibling pairs share both haplotypes by chance.

options.text: That type 1 diabetes is caused by HLA alone
options.rationale: Incorrect. Identical twins are concordant only about half the time; other genes and environment matter.
Incorrect. Excess sharing is a consistent, expected finding in type 1 diabetes families.

questions.stem: Which statement about HLA-DQB1*06:02 is correct?

options.text: A negative result makes narcolepsy with cataplexy very unlikely, while a positive result does not establish the diagnosis
options.rationale: Correct. More than 98% of patients carry it, but so do about 20% of healthy Europeans.

options.text: Its haplotype with DRB1*15:01 strongly increases type 1 diabetes risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. DRB1*15:01-DQB1*06:02 is strongly protective against type 1 diabetes.

options.text: Nearly all patients with narcolepsy without cataplexy carry it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only about 30–50% of type 2 narcolepsy patients carry it.

options.text: Carrying two copies lowers narcolepsy risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. Homozygosity doubled the risk in a European study.

claims.text: Expected sibling IBD sharing; affected sib-pair logic; LOD definition and thresholds.
HLA linkage in T1D (LOD 213.2); risk and protective haplotypes; twin concordance; HLA share of familial clustering.
DQB1*06:02 frequency in narcolepsy with cataplexy vs controls, NPV, homozygosity, protective alleles, type 2 frequency.
Observed 60/35/5 HLA sharing in diabetic sib pairs and its closeness to a recessive 100/0/0 pattern; reviewer’s 15–25% DQB1*06:02 population range.
claims.note: Specific sharing figures not found in an open source read this session; only qualitative excess sharing is taught. The reviewer’s 15–25% carrier range was also not found verbatim; Miyagawa 2019 gives 12–25% for the DRB1*15:01-DQB1*06:02 haplotype in European and East Asian general populations and Tafti 2014 gives 20% for DQB1*06:02 in Europe, so the lesson teaches about 20% for Europe.

claims.text: “One is noise, three is news”; “06:02 double agent”.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 51 Hit 8 gives monozygotic twin concordance in type 1 diabetes as ≤50%. Pociot 2010 estimates about 50%, but Noble 2011 reports 65% concordance by age 60 with long follow-up; the figure depends on follow-up length.

Ch. 51 Hit 5 states an NPV >99% for DQB1*06:02 testing in narcolepsy without naming the type. The 99.32% figure comes from narcolepsy with cataplexy (type 1) and was calculated from a European case-control sample of 1,218 patients and 3,541 controls (Tafti 2014), so it is not a general-population predictive value; only 30–50% of type 2 patients carry the allele (Miyagawa 2019).
